name: ME to WE
line: Over 3,000 girls and boys in thirteen years. Over 200 came back as peer leaders.
deck: It started in 2007 as a volunteer school on the banks of the Yamuna. Some of the children who came to it are now core team members here.

Alumni who came back as peer leaders

aims.p: The objective is to be the organisation still in these streets in ten years, rather than the one that reached more children in five.

aims.h: Move a child from what I need to what we do
aims.p: The name is the objective. There is no session at which it happens and no form on which it can be recorded.

aims.h: Still be useful after the last exam
aims.p: School stops and the questions get harder. The aim since 2019 has been to be reachable at that point rather than a memory of it.
Peer leadership is the intended end state. The measure is how much of this keeps running when we are not the ones running it.

how.p: A volunteer school on the Yamuna's banks in 2007. It became ME to WE in 2009, and the name is the method: the work moves from what I need to what we do.
The children come from Jagdamba Camp, Sheikh Sarai. The same settlement, the same families, year after year — which is why a fourteen-year-old here has usually known us since they were seven.

how.h: Then it follows them out of school
how.p: Since 2019, over four hundred young people through job-exposure camps. That is the part of the programme that starts where school stops, and it is where staying with one settlement pays off.
Over two hundred returned as peer leaders. A programme partly run by the people it was built for is not a nice detail — it is the only version of this that survives us losing interest.

who.h: Children from Jagdamba Camp, Sheikh Sarai
who.p: One settlement in south Delhi. Not a catchment and not a district — a set of streets and the same families in them.
Over two hundred alumni returned as peer leaders. They are both who this is for and who runs it.
The job-exposure camps are for the ones who have finished with school and are not finished with us. That group is on this list because they asked, not because we designed for them first.
Our own account says some of the children from the riverbank school are core team members here. It is the most self-interested line on this page and the one we would least like to lose.

done.h: Three thousand children, thirteen years, one settlement
done.p: Over 3,000 girls and boys, and over 200 of them back as peer leaders.
Our own sentence for it is that some are now core team members at Swechha. It is the best sentence in our account of ourselves and it is the one we can least prove.

done.h: One funder, for over a decade
done.p: EMpower has supported the work since 2014. Long money is rarer than large money and it is the reason a programme can stay in one settlement.

holes.what: The photograph above is one of ours and it is of schoolchildren, but it is not of this. Nothing of the riverbank school, nothing of the Jagdamba group, and no face on the alumni who became staff.
holes.unlocks: Any frame from the camp or the riverbank, with consent, and this page stops being the best-written unillustrated thing on the site.

holes.what: We say some alumni are now core team members and we name none of them.
holes.unlocks: Two names, with their permission. It would turn the strongest claim we make about ourselves into a person a reader can look at.

holes.what: ME to WE and She Leads Change both sit on Jagdamba and both run with EMpower. This page does not yet say how they differ.
holes.unlocks: One sentence of difference — or an answer that they are one programme, which is also fine, and shorter.

statement.line: Some of them work here now.
statement.under: There is no list of names behind it, which is why it is a sentence on this page and not a figure.
